sections.title: Activity: imagine or remember safety cues

blocks.p: Sensory safety anchors use your five senses. (Those are smell, taste, touch, sight, and hearing if you need a reminder.) These five senses take information from the external environment and send it to your brainstem. Your brainstem makes neuroceptive detections and shifts your body's state based on what it identifies as safe, dangerous, or life-threatening. It then sends those signals to the rest of your brain and down to your body as well.
Let's return to the quote from Dr. Porges:

q: "Once the passive pathway effectively shifts our physiological state, the second step can be initiated. The second step, exercising the vagal brake, recruits the active (voluntary) pathway through rituals requiring manipulation of breath, posture, and vocalization." (Porges)

blocks.p: Passive sensory cues will provide the foundation to shift your autonomic state toward more safety. Passive safety cueing opens the possibility of using active safety cueing, anchoring, and strengthening your vagal brake.

Our senses are constantly providing cues of safety or danger to our brainstem, whether we consciously experience them or not. Background sensory neuroception provides an excellent opportunity to increase consistent safety cues. On top of the passive cues, sensory inputs provide an opportunity for active safety anchoring through mindfulness of their experiences.

The senses are great for reducing defensive activation as well, like reducing anxiety through calming music. I've also found mindfully using sensory safety cues helps reduce dissociation in clients. And soft lighting can help someone in shutdown to come back to the present moment.

You can probably already see how passive sensory anchors directly connect with the environment. In [the environment anchor](piece:anchor-environment), I asked you to identify one spot in your home that would serve as a Passive Safety Environment. This is where you'll focus your attention with sensory anchors. The Passive Safety Environment provides a constant stream of passive safety cues. These will form a foundation for eventually practicing active safety anchors, like movement-based ones. The Passive Safety Environment is also ideal for mindfully experiencing the passive safety cues you cultivate there.

While senses can be great options for passive and active safety, keep in mind they can act as defensive triggers as well. If you have been through something traumatic, you may still get triggered by some aspect of that event, especially if your body went into a freeze state. As your body entered that immobilized state of freeze, it still neurocepted through the senses. In that moment, it identified sensory aspects of the environment and associated them with life-threat.

This association is not because your system is defective. "Really, Justin? Because it seems like quite the opposite." Yes, really. Your wonderful body is associating the life-threatening circumstance with the surrounding environmental pieces. It neurocepts those sensory inputs as life-threats. In the future, you're more likely to survive when neurocepting those life-threatening pieces. This is evolutionarily advantageous when accurately neurocepting dangerous cues from the environment.

Imagine you're a mouse, and you need to eat. You come out of your mouse hole in the wall and into the main house, where some cheese sits on a table. Everything seems normal, so you concoct some scheme to scurry up the table legs to get the cheese. Halfway up the leg, a grandfather clock gongs and wakes up "Tom," the guardian house cat. Tom sees and attacks you, but you escape and get back into the hole in the wall, using your sympathetic flight energy.

You survive. You're not traumatized since you successfully used the flight activation to get away. But now, your system will identify the gong of the grandfather clock with the cat waking up, and with danger. And this new association of the gong with danger will help you to survive the next time. If you hear the gong, you will shift into a defensive state and be better prepared to escape and survive. However, since you are not traumatized, the gong will not send you into a dysregulated spiral in a benign context, like when you're inside your hole-in-the-wall home.

But we both know that sensory stimuli can indeed send someone into a dysregulated spiral as a result of a traumatic event. Let's say Tom caught you, slamming his paw on your tail as you attempted to flee. He's immobilized you while your flight/fight state is active. You're unable to successfully use your sympathetic flight/fight state and return to the safety of the hole in the wall. This immobilization of flight/fight results in a stuck freeze defensive state. The stuck freeze lingers in your body, potentially for years. When you hear the gong, your present-day state triggers back to the immobilization from Tom; your flight/fight activation ready to burst, even if Tom is not around. (That's just one sensory aspect of the traumatizing event. There is a long list of potential others.)

We're hardwired to respond to our sensory input in largely predictable ways. We have reflexes, like blinking when something is too close to our eyes or pulling back when burned. These are general and predictable. But our senses also create individualized imprints of danger to increase our chances of survival. I think of them as "neuroceptive tattoos." When the mouse hears the gong, it triggers freeze. Just like the soldier who survived a war environment is triggered into freeze when he hears the boom of fireworks. Those sensory stimuli, the gong and the firework booms, are neuroceptively "tattooed" onto these individuals due to the association of those sensory stimuli with a traumatic context. Those sounds will not induce the same response in someone else because they don't have the same traumatic association.

As you attempt to notice what sensory inputs ground you in safety, I invite you to do so with curiosity and without judgment. You may notice a certain smell grounds you in safety, but another feels too similar to some past context that takes you away from safety. For now, it's enough to notice and take a mental note of. It's not because you're defective. It might be one of those "neuroceptive tattoos," especially if the scent sends you into dysregulation. If you stumble upon one of these, it may help to use a coping skill you know already works, like distracting yourself, getting mobile, changing your environment, or all of the above.

You and I will have different sensory safety cues, not just because we're unique individuals with varying safety experiences. But also because we will have more or less access to these sensory potentials. I generally have a terrible sense of smell, and I need to wear glasses for better vision. I still have access to these senses but with a limited capacity. You will have to notice your capacity for using each of your senses. One sense may be easily accessible, while another is not.

Lilly was chronically in an extreme dissociative shutdown. She had basically zero awareness of her internal world, like her emotions. So, we started with her external environment. But she quickly recognized she struggled with that as well. The only sensory input that triggered safety in her was through touch, which she used on a super soft blanket at home. That was her starting point for accessing safety because, well, that's all she had.

As you become curious about what sensory inputs bring you to safety, also be mindful of what takes you away from safety. In your safety environment, do what you can to increase the safety cues and decrease the danger cues. Things in the environment may take you away from safety to a noticeable degree but don't trigger your stuck trauma, like the hum of the A/C or traffic in the background. Or maybe the dogs across the street won't stop barking, even when you're trying to record a podcast episode. (Okay, that might just be my own experience.)

What triggers your defensive activation won't be the same as mine. I can't tell you what to add or remove from your safety environment. Be curious about what your senses tell you. Listen to the little pulls toward safety and the pushes away from danger. However, some sensory stimuli may be predictably more of a safety or danger cue.

I'm willing to bet that you will feel more safety with the sound of waves than you would with the sound of pots and pans banging together. So, you should lean toward introducing the sound of waves into your Passive Safety Environment. And you're probably going to feel safer with consistent lighting than you would with flashing lights. So, it would make sense to ensure you have consistent lighting. And the scent of lavender is very likely more safety-inducing than the smell of… well, fill in the blank here with whatever you like.

You get the idea. Some things are predictably safer than others. But within those obvious examples, your individual experience will differ. You may like the sound of waves, but another person likes the sound of a waterfall and another person likes the sound of dripping water. You may love consistent lighting, but want a soft yellowish light while another person would like a cooler white. You may love lavender and another likes vanilla.
Okay, this makes sense to you and you're on board. But where to start? We look for clues!

Whatever brings you to your safety state through your imagination or from the real world provides a clue as to what you can use in your Passive Safety Environment at home. You may already know that a green forest or the calm rhythm of beach waves cues safety for your body. You can use the sensory experience of these environments within your home.

"But Justin, I don't have a forest outside of my home! And there's no beach out there either!" Yeah, me neither. So, we may not have direct access to these things. However, we can still learn from these environments that we feel safe in. We can find clues from them and then integrate aspects of them into the safety environment at home. Let's return to the [imaginary safety environment exercise](piece:recognize-polyvagal-safety#using-your-imagination-to-explore-safety) and see what clues we can find there.

blocks.h3: Activity: imagine or remember safety cues

blocks.p: Take a moment to imagine or remember a safety environment. It can be something you make up, a place you've been, or a place you would like to go. Once you have it, spend a moment immersed in the sensory aspects of the environment, then answer these questions in your journal:

ul: What do you see that provides a safety cue?
What do you smell that provides a safety cue?
What do you hear that provides a safety cue?
What do you touch that provides a safety cue?
What do you taste that provides a safety cue?

blocks.p: Here are my answers, based on my safety environment of a small cabin in the woods:

ol: What do you see that provides a safety cue? Shade, tall green trees, and sunlight speckled on the ground; viewing through a large window; a black mug in hand.
What do you smell that provides a safety cue? Trees, clean air, coffee or tea.
What do you hear that provides a safety cue? Lots and lots of peaceful silence, natural sounds.

What do you touch that provides a safety cue? My bottom sits on a chair; hand is holding a simple black ceramic mug, heat of the coffee or tea on my hand, the light weight of the knitted throw blanket across my legs.
What do you taste that provides a safety cue? Coffee with caramel or cinnamon. Or Egyptian Licorice tea.

blocks.p: The next step is identifying which elements we can realistically bring into our safety environment. I can't bring the shade of the forest. But can I dim the lights in my safety environment? Sure. I can't bring the silence of it either. But can I dampen the noise around me and turn off things creating hums? Yep. I can also get a black coffee mug from the kitchen and have the warmth of whatever is inside. Can I drape a blanket across my legs in my safety environment? You betcha. I can also get a forest-scented candle and let natural sunlight into my space.

During my first session with Sascha, she identified a beach, an imaginary safety place with sunlight, rhythmic wave sounds, the water itself, and warmth. Sascha used this feeling of safety to inspire a post-session homework assignment of going to a lake and mindfully walking around it. She further used these imaginative pieces in her home safety environment by allowing natural light in through the window and getting a small fountain for her work desk, which provided her with constant sounds of water. She added bright tropical pinks and greens to her Passive Safety Environment.
Now it's your turn. Which sensory inputs from the activity can you bring to your home safety environment? What can you control within your environment to add a bit more safety to it?

Setting up your Passive Safety Environment is great for laying a safety foundation. You may notice that simply doing this already makes you feel more safety in your system. You might be able to get more work done in this area or just come here to breathe easier. But you can go a step further.

Once you have passive safety cues in your home, the next step is to mindfully and actively utilize sensory anchors. The sensory anchors you actively use could be the same ones that you have set up for passive safety cues. For example, if you have a candle scent to provide passive cues, you can intentionally shift your conscious attention to that sensory experience. As you do, actively notice how your body responds to the scent. Ask yourself the same three questions -

ol: When I do _, am I more or less likely to smile?
Is my breathing more or less comfortable when I _?
Do my muscles get more or less tense when I _?

blocks.p: Take the time to truly feel and consciously recognize what it feels like to activate your safety state through all of your senses. This mindful engagement increases the likelihood of replicating and building upon that feeling of safety. It strengthens your safety foundation and also adds safety reference points you can call upon later. For now, use your senses to activate safety within your Passive Safety Environment. As things get easier, practice them outside of this environment.

We are inundated with sensory stimuli all the time. Right now, there is probably something that you are seeing, feeling, and hearing. You might also be tasting and smelling something, too. Not only is there one thing for each of these senses, but there are probably multiple things simultaneously. As I write this in my therapy office, I can hear the dull traffic outside, the white noise machine, the beep of the door opening, and the internet installer carrying his ladder by my door. Sensory overload takes you out of present moment connection and may even bump you out of a firmer anchoring in your safety state. Much of this you can't control. But you can control some aspects of your home environment. And you can control where you focus your mindful attention. If you don't purposefully focus on safety, you remain a passive and reflexive recipient of sensory overwhelm.

Slow down and notice what your senses are telling you. You just might be surprised at how much information is sent to your brainstem through each sensory input and how much we consciously miss out on. For example, imagine looking at a pink rose. You see the rose, yes. But there is more to see than just the rose. If you slow down, you can notice the smaller details of what your eyes are sensing, like the pink of the rose. Or the highlights of the sun hitting the petals and the soft shadows they cast onto the petals beneath them. You may notice a ladybug hanging out inside the rose, the thorns on the stem, or a drop of morning dew.

The rose is not just a rose. There are many pieces to the visual experience, each providing you with a neuroception of safety or danger. The pink might trigger a sense of vibrancy and playfulness. Or maybe it's too much, and a softer yellow brings you more safety. The ladybug might trigger curiosity, but it also might trigger an "Ick!" But you won't know unless you slow down and notice each of these sensory pieces in smaller detail. These small details provide unique experiences you can feel in your body if you pay attention.

As you practice mindfully experiencing each sensory input, you may attain more appreciation for what your senses are picking up one at a time. But you may also have more appreciation for the collective sensory experience. I encourage you to be purposeful, slow down, and take it in. Notice what you like and dislike.
Stay in the moment with mindfulness.
"Seriously, Justin? Again with the mindfulness?"

"Yes, again with the mindfulness!" I know; I keep talking about it. But I only do so because it's really important. If you can stay in the present moment through mindfulness, it will help prevent spiraling into a dysregulated time-travel retraumatization. Let me explain.

In a way, our senses can take us back in time. Remember, your brainstem may receive sensory inputs associated with a prior life-threatening experience, causing it to shift into a defensive state from the past. Or trigger a currently stuck defensive state. After the brainstem neurocepts and shifts state, your body and brain might vividly re-experience the memory.

When triggered, it's really difficult to notice these shifts and then come back to the present moment. So when it comes to sensory and other anchors, focus on the present moment experience. If any practice brings up past discomfort, give yourself permission to pause and return when ready, or try another practice.

If you can stay in the present moment, that's a good indication that you are accessing and maintaining your safety state. Maintaining access to the present moment is a great sign that your safety state is strengthening. Maintaining could be for just a few seconds or something longer. There is no right amount of time. If it's longer than you were able to before, then you're probably on the right track. To gauge your level of present-moment connection, ask yourself questions like this:

ul: Do I feel connected to the present moment?
Do I feel more connected to my body?
Am I able to notice my sensory experience?
Am I thinking about now or some other time?
Are the feelings I have connected to the present or some other time?
Am I able to breathe into my belly softly?

blocks.why: Short bursts of mindful sensing, daily. This practice is one of those bursts, through sound. (Change the sense in the practice if another suits you better.)

blocks.p: Use sensory anchors daily. Use them in short bursts of mindful awareness and try to find new sensory inputs that activate your safety state. At a minimum, try to be more curious about what your senses tell you and purposefully look for safety from them. Use your mindful sensing a couple of times per day. Then, ask yourself those safety assessment questions again.
Let's do a quick present-moment sensory exercise in your immediate environment. Right now, focus on your senses and what they're telling you.

ul: What is your taste telling you?
What are you detecting in your touch? (Are you sitting on something? Are your hands touching something? Can you feel your clothes on your skin?)
How about in your hearing? (Can you hear things close by? How about further away? Can you hear the silence under the noises?)
What are you detecting in your sight besides this screen?
What are you smelling?

blocks.p: Now reflect or journal on these:

ul: What senses do you typically find the most grounding? What stimulates that sense? Let yourself remember and feel that experience for a moment.

blocks.p: Research options on grounding through your senses. Here are some starting points:

ul: The "5-4-3-2-1" method
Search for scents to calm down
Search for using the eyes to calm down
What is ASMR?

ol: Focus on what you can access in your senses and then make the most of those senses to build on your strengths.

Mindfully use your senses. These are potentially the best ways to return to the present moment if needed. But for now, just mindfully experience what it feels like to be in safety through your senses.
Your senses are a direct connection to your neuroception process. So bring in more passive safety cues through your senses, then use them actively.

blocks.prompt: Did this provide you with any new experiences of safety?
Was this challenging for you? What about it was challenging?
Is this something you can continue to practice?
What three sensory stimuli did you find the most beneficial? Is there something they have in common?

blocks.p: You may not have found something yet that is noticeably activating your safety state. You may have tried many things over the years to get relief and now believe that nothing works and nothing will work.

You're not alone. [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) students don't always find something that immediately works for them, either. When you live in a traumatized state, it's not easy to find and feel safety.
Has nothing worked? Maybe.
Will nothing work? Doubtful.

Activating the ventral pathways and feeling safe and connected is generally possible. But yes, it's difficult when stuck in trauma. Your unfruitful efforts can cause frustration and maybe even cause you to lose hope.

If this is you, your best action might be to focus your efforts on your environment. I want you to keep learning, at the very least. But continue to focus your efforts on your environment. Increasing your passive safety cues might be the best you can do right now.

And there is nothing wrong with that. If safety is new to your system, it needs nurturance. It will get more accustomed to the ventral pathways, and safety will eventually be less difficult. Eventually, you will be conscious of it and feel it when you look inward.

If looking inward for safety is difficult, focus more on what you like or dislike. For example, the next time you're at your favorite department store, smell a candle and ask yourself if you like it or not. The next time you lay on your bed, ask yourself if you like the feel of your sheets or not. The next time you eat, ask yourself if you like the taste or not.

As you identify things you like, spend more time experiencing the sensations of liking that thing. If it's a taste, chew a little slower. If it's a scent, inhale a bit deeper. And if it's a texture, touch a little longer. And do so more mindfully, focusing on the felt experience of it.
And even if you're not frustrated with your progress, it's probably still a good idea to slow down and notice these sensory pieces in your daily life. Slow down. Notice. Repeat.
